title: Eutychus falls asleep (Acts 20:1–16)
hookLine: Paul preaches till midnight, a young man dozes off in a window, and is restored
carry: they were not a little comforted
tomorrow: Paul's last words to his friends are words of Jesus. which ones?

lines: A HEAD IN THE BACK ROW, DIPPING.
cards: Every teacher knows the sight: a head in the back row dipping, catching itself, dipping again. Maybe you've been that head once or twice. Troas, the first day of the week.

The believers have gathered to break bread, and Paul, who leaves in the morning, "continued his speech until midnight." Then Acts adds a detail that seems to go nowhere: "there were many lights in the upper chamber."
Why tell us about the lamps? Because a young man is sitting in the window, and he's fading.

teach.b: "And there sat in a window a certain young man named Eutychus, being fallen into a deep sleep: and as Paul was long preaching, he sunk down with sleep, and fell down from the third loft, and was taken up dead."
So, the lamps. Acts never says why it mentions them. Some readers hear a gentle explanation tucked into the scene: a crowded room, many flames, a late hour, a long talk.
And look at the phrase as Paul was long preaching. The text practically takes the young man's side. His tiredness isn't treated as a sin.
Paul stops. He goes down, throws himself on the young man, and holds him.
"Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him." Readers weigh that line differently: some hear a raising from the dead, others hear Paul finding life still there. Either way, see what happens next.
Paul goes back up, breaks bread, eats, and keeps talking "a long while, even till break of day." No lecture about staying awake.
And the last line goes to the people in the room: "And they brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted."
Here's the one to tell a friend: the young man who nodded off becomes the reason a whole room goes home comforted.

how: Christians read the story of Eutychus in Acts 20; some note that the believers there gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, and some churches point to it when they gather on Sundays.

s: Acts tells this story as a warning against sleeping in church
no one scolds him. Acts says he sank down as Paul was long preaching.
after the fall, Paul kept talking until daybreak
he broke bread and talked a long while, even till break of day.
Acts explains that the lamps made the room stuffy

games.q: your grandpa nods off during your sister's piano recital. afterward she's furious and wants you to back her up. what fits Eutychus?
o: remind her gently that he came, and the night was long.
agree he was rude, and say he owes her an apology.
suggest he skip the next one if he's that tired.
games.why: Acts puts the long sermon in the sentence, not blame on the sleeper, and ends with a room not a little comforted.

practice: Count on your fingers the tired people who showed up for you lately: someone who drove you after a long shift, sat through your thing half-asleep, answered a late text.
Give each one a finger and a quiet thank-you; tired people who came anyway still came. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Eutychus falls asleep. A young man in a window, a sermon past midnight, and a fall that ends in comfort.

orig.note: Greek: the young man's name in Acts 20:9.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: they were not a little comforted, which is old English for a great deal. Sleep well.
